event_overview.title: About Slavery Reparations
event_overview.subject: Slavery Reparations
event_overview.summary: Slavery reparations refers to efforts to obtain acknowledgment, redress and remedial action for the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans, racialized chattel slavery, colonialism and their continuing effects on people of African descent. The issue is pursued through international human-rights interpretation, national and regional policy, diplomacy, and—in some cases—proposed or actual legal proceedings; proposals can include apologies, truth-telling, education, restitution, development measures, compensation and guarantees against recurrence.

facts.label: International framework
facts.value: The UN World Conference against Racism, held in Durban, South Africa, from 31 August to 7 September 2001, produced the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, which recognizes slavery and the slave trade as crimes against humanity and links their legacy to present-day racism and discrimination.

facts.label: Treaty basis and oversight
facts.value: The International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD) was adopted on 21 December 1965 and entered into force on 4 January 1969. Its implementation is monitored by the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), an independent-expert treaty body; the UN treaty record listed 182 States parties as of 21 July 2026.

facts.label: UN guidance adopted in 2026
facts.value: At its 118th session in Geneva in August 2026, CERD adopted General Recommendation No. 40 on reparatory justice for harms and continuing consequences of colonialism, trafficking in enslaved Africans and racialized slavery. The Committee described the guidance as grounded in ICERD and as addressing structural inequality, truth-telling, historical memory, education, participation, accountability and non-recurrence, rat

facts.label: Caribbean regional agenda
facts.value: CARICOM’s Reparations Commission frames reparatory justice as a regional reconciliation and development agenda. Its Ten Point Plan includes a formal apology, repatriation, Indigenous peoples’ development, cultural institutions, public-health and education initiatives, technology transfer, psychological rehabilitation and debt cancellation.

facts.label: Jamaica-related context
facts.value: CARICOM Heads of Government approved an updated regional reparations manifesto in July 2026 and backed Jamaica’s planned filing of a reparations petition to King Charles III in London on 7 September 2026, placing that action within the wider Caribbean reparatory-justice campaign.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline tracks selected recent UN and Jamaica-related developments in the reparations debate; it does not provide a comprehensive history of slavery, an inventory of all reparations claims, or a record of every national policy or court case.
